content: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are infections that develop in wounds following surgical procedures. Preoperative bathing or showering with an antiseptic skin wash, such as chlorhexidine gluconate, is a widely accepted practice aimed at reducing the number of bacteria (microflora) on the skin. However, it remains uncertain whether reducing skin microflora directly translates to a lower risk of developing SSIs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the effectiveness of preoperative bathing or showering with antiseptic agents in preventing hospital-acquired SSIs. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared the use of antiseptic preparations for full-body preoperative bathing or showering with non-antiseptic preparations in surgical patients. For this fifth update, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and reference lists was conducted up to December 18, 2014. Seven trials involving a total of 10,157 participants were included in the analysis. The antiseptic used in all the trials was 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (Hibiscrub or Riohex). Four of the trials included three comparison groups. Three trials, involving 7,791 participants, compared bathing with chlorhexidine to bathing with a placebo. The results showed no statistically significant reduction in SSIs when chlorhexidine was used instead of a placebo. The relative risk (RR) of developing an SSI in this comparison was 0.91, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.80 to 1.04. When only high-quality trials were considered, the RR was 0.95 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.10), again showing no significant difference. Three trials, involving 1,443 participants, compared the use of bar soap to chlorhexidine. When the results of these trials were combined, there was no significant difference in the risk of SSIs between the two groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.84). Three additional trials, involving 1,192 participants, compared bathing with chlorhexidine to no preoperative washing at all. One large study in this group found a statistically significant reduction in SSIs in favor of bathing with chlorhexidine (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.79). However, the smaller studies in this group did not find any significant difference between patients who bathed with chlorhexidine and those who did not wash preoperatively. In conclusion, this review found no clear evidence to support the use of preoperative bathing or showering with chlorhexidine over other washing products to reduce the risk of SSIs. Efforts to lower the incidence of hospital-acquired SSIs should focus on interventions that have demonstrated clear effectiveness.
